title: The point receives a push
subject: Force, mass, retained velocity
story: Meet the familiar sphere on a quiet test lane. Bring the point class and its body from earlier halls; add a finite push while gravity and damping are deliberately disabled. Let go and watch it continue. Repeat with twice the mass and the same shape, force and duration. The student changes the pulse and predicts the resulting motion. The sphere leaves this encounter as a receiver with state, ready to pass the same question to the player.
carry: Point appearance and construction → dynamic sphere with known mass and velocity.
variation: Choose a different duration and predict the change of velocity before running it.
test: Known pulse matches Δv = F × duration / mass within declared numerical tolerance; release clears push only; double mass halves Δv.
reflection: The command ends. Its consequence has not.
short: IN point body. ADD finite push, mass. SEE continued motion after release. VARY duration. OUT force receiver. TEST Δv; release; mass.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed sphere study adapted from the existing Motion hall. Disable gravity and damping for this comparison. Arrow lengths are schematic, not measured ratios.

title: You become the launched body
subject: Launch velocity, impulse distinction, gravity
story: Walk onto one launch pad and cross a small gap. Begin with the sphere's previous response, then inspect the player's receiver: the installed pad sets velocity, while an impulse model would add a mass-dependent change. Introduce constant downward acceleration through the visible arc. Change one launch component, compare a prediction with the actual landing, and reset at the pad. A second pad asks the student to reach a higher ledge using the same rule. Carry gravity and outgoing velocity into flight.
carry: Known sphere response → explicit player receiver, one launch event.
variation: Reach a different ledge by changing vertical launch speed while keeping horizontal speed fixed.
test: Launch occurs once per entry; model gravity matches receiver; no hidden mid-flight velocity lock or landing teleport in the free-flight variant.
reflection: An arrow becomes a route your body must finish.
short: IN sphere response. ADD player receiver, one launch, gravity. VARY vertical speed. OUT airborne velocity. TEST single event; actual landing; no hidden lock.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed free-flight course. Existing pad implementations must be checked: setting velocity and applying an impulse are different operations. The large gaps establish the visual idea; they are not a tested VR course.

title: Two points can carry you
subject: Vector addition, continuous thrust, net force
story: Hold one familiar sphere in each hand over a low flight court. Hold each trigger for thrust opposite the controller's aim: point down to lift, back to advance. This is the author's chosen control. Start with one hand, then add the other through the same receiver. Aim together, apart and in opposition; combine thrust with gravity rather than replacing it. Releasing a trigger removes its thrust while motion continues. The student tunes a pair of contributions to hover or travel sideways. Both hands use instances of the same object; the new lesson is their sum.
carry: Launch + gravity → controllable contributions to the player's acceleration.
variation: Choose unequal hand strengths that produce a stated horizontal direction while balancing weight.
test: Aim down gives upward thrust; aim back gives forward thrust. Both inputs reach one update; order does not change their sum; releasing a trigger or dropping a sphere clears only its contribution. Opposite horizontal thrust leaves gravity; level camera; one-hand/desktop adapter uses the same contributions.
reflection: Cooperation need not mean that both hands do the same thing.
short: IN player receiver. ADD two point instances, held thrust sum. INPUT accepted: aim down/back + hold triggers → up/forward. RELEASE clears own thrust only. VARY direction/strength. OUT steering. TEST sum before update; gravity/velocity retained.
caption: New concept illustration: The control is agreed. Two-sphere player flight remains to be implemented and tested. White streams indicate aim; amber arrows indicate the resulting thrust in the opposite direction.

title: Release is not a stop
subject: Gravity, velocity-dependent drag, opposing thrust
story: Leave the launch ledge and release both triggers. You keep travelling as gravity bends the path downward. Add a clearly marked drag volume, then compare it with deliberate counter-thrust from the spheres. The student chooses a drag coefficient and observes a changed approach to the landing zone. Make repeated short falls with nearby restart points; do not secretly arrest the body when the trigger ends. What is learned here will make entry to the vortex legible.
carry: Existing velocity + gravity + thrust → explicit resistance term.
variation: Land in the same zone using early weak braking and later stronger braking; compare the routes.
test: Trigger release zeros thrust only; drag opposes current velocity and does nonpositive work in the isolated check; full player model retains gravity and collisions.
reflection: Freedom to move includes the problem of coming to rest.
short: IN flight state. ADD Fdrag=-b*v. COMPARE release, passive drag, counter-thrust. OUT controlled landing. TEST thrust reset only; drag direction.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed short-fall and braking encounter, with nearby resets. Drag and counter-thrust need separate comparisons. A released sphere emits no thrust stream. A backward force does not instantly reverse a forward velocity.

title: The room turns your path
subject: Position-dependent field, radial and tangential contributions
story: Enter a broad court where the same sphere and the visitor meet a swirling field. Reuse vector subtraction to find the centre and add an inward and tangential contribution. Carry incoming velocity through the field instead of resetting it on entry. The student changes one component, sees the spiral change and uses the held spheres to escape or enter a chosen landing lane. Compare this with the old velocity-assignment vortex so the difference between directing motion and changing motion remains visible.
carry: Accumulated velocity → field contribution sampled at current position.
variation: Remove only the inward component and predict how entry and escape change.
test: Incoming velocity is retained; radial term points inward and tangent is perpendicular; centre handling stays finite; exit removes field contribution without clearing velocity.
reflection: A centre can gather bodies without becoming their rightful destination.
short: IN receiver state. ADD field(position), radial+tangent. VARY one term. OUT field navigation. TEST centre finite; entry/exit preserve velocity. Old vortex assigns v.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed force-accumulating vortex. The installed velocity-setting vortex is a comparison, not evidence of this behavior. The inset distinguishes radial and tangential directions. The scene does not prescribe one orbit for every incoming body.

title: Send the push to another body
subject: Projectile contact, one-off impulse, mass response
story: Return the sphere to its familiar catalyst role and send a small form across a target lane. One impact delivers one declared impulse to a dynamic sphere. Repeat with equal-size light and heavy receivers, then let one receiver approach under a bounded force so the student can divert it. The shot changes a body's motion before it changes a score. Thrust and firing have explicit, separate controls or an explicit mode choice; pressing the same trigger must not unexpectedly launch both player and projectile.
carry: Held point + projectile appearance + known mass law → collision receiver.
variation: Choose an impulse that gives two different masses the same desired velocity change.
test: One contact applies J once; passive receiver satisfies Δv=J/m; no extra collision impulse is double-counted; lifetime and reset work; pursuit disabled during mass comparison.
reflection: A body can obstruct you without its only possible future being destruction or obedience.
short: IN catalyst form + mass. ADD one hit→impulse receiver. VARY J,m. OUT deflection. TEST single hit; no double impulse; passive comparison. Separate FIRE/THRUST.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed dynamic sphere target and bounded pursuit variant. Flight and firing require separate actions or an explicit mode. The mass comparison uses free receivers and disables pursuit. Pedestals in the illustration identify the specimens; they are not a constraint model.

title: Give the body a place to return to
subject: Restoring force, displacement from an anchor, damping
story: Meet the same target sphere with a visible tether to an anchor. Shoot it aside and watch the retained velocity carry it past the resting place. Add the spring contribution to the already learned damping term. The student changes the anchor or stiffness, then uses the altered sweep to cross a passage. Start with a one-axis study before the spatial enemy. Carry a state-dependent force into the last course and leave a clear opening into Waves.
carry: Dynamic sphere + impulse + drag → restoring force toward an explicit anchor.
variation: Move the anchor without changing the sphere's shape and predict the new resting place.
test: Spring term is zero at anchor and opposes displacement; damping still opposes velocity; same law drives study and enemy; numerical step stable at chosen parameters.
reflection: What is asking the body to return—and who put its centre there?
short: IN target + drag. ADD Fspring=-k*(x-anchor). VARY anchor/k. OUT return/overshoot. TEST zero/sign; damping; stable step. Bridge Waves.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed tethered enemy variant from the existing spring study. Begin with a one-dimensional guide. The last panel sketches anchor placement. A spring moving freely in space requires additional constraints; it is not the first one-dimensional model.

title: Take the abilities through the room
subject: Composition of learned forces and interaction states
story: Cross one connected museum level: short jump pads, an open flight well, a vortex edge, a falling passage, a rolling target and a tethered obstruction. Keep nearby restart points and a ground route for inspection. The student alters one familiar parameter to make another route possible and explains its consequences. The final course introduces no new compulsory force law: the sphere's accumulated abilities are enough. An optional sentry adds aim and deflection only after those abilities work independently.
carry: All previous abilities → one traversable encounter; documented sphere state carried onward.
variation: Make a second successful route by changing one field or pad parameter and explain the tradeoff.
test: Pad/hand/field contributions share the movement owner; all gates clear on exit/restart; no required enemy conversion; test ordinary, one-hand and desktop traversal separately.
reflection: The museum now depends on capacities you have made, without demanding a single correct path.
short: IN all abilities. ADD no law. COMPOSE pads, flight, swirl, fall, targets. VARY route. OUT capable point/player. TEST restart; handoff; alternate traversal.
caption: New concept illustration: Proposed combined course. No new force law belongs here; the test is whether earlier abilities remain usable together. Cyan lines here are route guides, not instantaneous velocity vectors. The architectural montage is not a verified traversable layout.
